title: Aurum Defense - On‑Prem / Air‑gapped Deployment Discovery
next_steps: Send SOC2 + security whitepaper and network diagram (Lena) by 2026-12-08
Prepare sized hardware options and cost delta for on‑prem A100 vs H100 node pools (Marcus) by 2026-12-10
Customer to share scope of data classified as CUI/ITAR and list of internal stakeholders (Rachel) by 2026-12-09

action_items: Lena Park: Share SOC2 report + security whitepaper (due 2026-12-08)

transcript:
Meeting header:
[00:00] Lena Park: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Lena from Redwood Inference. Marcus, my SE, is with me.
[00:07] Rachel Kim: Hey thanks, yeah we've been looking at Redwood, excited to chat — I'm Rachel, CTO at Aurum.
[00:12] Marcus Vela: Hi Rachel, Derek, Anita. Quick agenda: confirm requirements for an air‑gapped on‑prem deployment, constraints (hardware, update process), security/compliance musts, and next steps.
[00:22] Derek Shaw: Great. To start, we operate in a defense environment, we have ITAR and some classified PII, we cannot have any egress — zero outbound to internet from the inference nodes.
[00:31] Anita Bose: Our infra is mostly Red Hat OpenShift, strict FIPS mode, HSM available via Thales Luna, and we currently run a mix of NVIDIA A100 and an older fleet of A40s.
[00:40] Lena Park: Ok that's helpful. Two quick clarifications: when you say "no egress", do you mean the control plane cannot reach Redwood hosted control plane at all, or minimal ephemeral connectivity for management?
[00:49] Rachel Kim: No connectivity allowed — procurement and cyber both locked that down. We're exploring a private deployment where control plane is customer‑managed or a fully offline install.
[00:57] Marcus Vela: Understood. Redwood supports a Private deployment that can run with a customer‑managed control plane and we also do an air‑gapped install using signed bundles. It's effectively an offline installer — we've done it for other regulated orgs.
[01:06] Derek Shaw: How do you handle updates? We can't have automatic outbound updates.
[01:10] Marcus Vela: We provide cryptographically signed update artifacts. For air‑gapped, we ship a signed tar bundle or OCI image that you import into your internal registry. Your security team verifies signatures; optional HSM can verify key signatures. We also have an offline validation checklist and a staging procedure.
[01:20] Anita Bose: That sounds reasonable. Does the private package include both the control plane and serving runtime?
[01:24] Lena Park: Yes — the package includes the control plane components (API gateway, admin UI, telemetry ingestion endpoints that can be pointed at internal observability) plus the serving runtime images. The runtime supports NVIDIA GPUs, and we offer CPU fallback.
[01:33] Rachel Kim: On GPUs — our finance team is pushing for cost efficiency. We have a small H100 pilot procurement coming in Q1 and more A100s after. Can Redwood run on H100 and A100, any perf differences?
[01:42] Marcus Vela: Short answer: yes. We validate on A100 and H100. H100 often gives better throughput/lower latency for certain transformer ops, but depends on sequence lengths and model variant. For planning we present two hardware profiles: A100‑based nodes and H100‑based nodes. We also provide quantization recommendations — 8‑bit, 4‑bit variants to reduce memory and cost.
[01:55] Derek Shaw: Would we need different kernels or compilers for H100 vs A100? We use tightly controlled OS images.
[02:00] Marcus Vela: There's some kernel/hypervisor dependency — the serving runtime uses vendor kernels/CUDA drivers. For RHEL/OpenShift you need the matching CUDA driver/kernel ABI. We provide an install matrix. For strict images we can work with your team to produce certified images or a reference OCI image you can mirror.
[02:12] Rachel Kim: What about model weights — can we host weights internally? We can't have any model artifacts sent outside.
[02:16] Lena Park: Absolutely. In Private/on‑prem deployments, model weights stay on your cluster; Redwood's control plane can be configured to never call home. We also support bringing your own model artifacts; if you want Redwood models, we deliver them as signed bundles you import.
[02:28] Anita Bose: Ok. On security controls: we need SAML SSO, RBAC, audit logs, and integration with our SIEM. Can you point logs to our Splunk/Elastic stack?
[02:36] Marcus Vela: Yes to SAML and RBAC. Logs can be forwarded to your SIEM; we provide structured audit logs and a fluentd/collector configuration for air‑gapped environments.
[02:44] Derek Shaw: Key management: we use a Thales HSM. Can Redwood integrate so that encryption keys never leave the HSM?
[02:50] Lena Park: We support KMS/HSM integrations; keys can be wrapped and the platform operates with key references. For offline installs we'll work with your HSM team — the license tokens and signed artifacts are validated using keys that can be provisioned inside the HSM.
[03:02] Rachel Kim: How do you handle telemetry and usage reporting? Our compliance team will not allow any identifiable telemetry to leave the network.
[03:07] Marcus Vela: For air‑gapped, telemetry is optional. You can opt into sending aggregated anonymized telemetry via an offline export process, or disable it entirely. We also have on‑prem observability dashboards.
[03:16] Anita Bose: Regarding acceptance testing: procurement wants a pass/fail benchmark for latency and throughput. Can you help run a benchmarking run on our hardware before we sign a contract?
[03:24] Lena Park: Yes — typical flow is: Redwood provides a benchmark harness and sample prompts, you run it in your environment on pinned model versions, and we review results. For air‑gapped we can send the harness as part of the signed bundle or run a remote‑assisted test where our SE walks you through the runbook over an encrypted call.
[03:36] Derek Shaw: What's the lead time for an air‑gapped install? We have a procurement window in Jan.
[03:40] Marcus Vela: For an initial pilot, typically 4‑8 weeks: legal/PO, security review, offline artifact packaging, and a staged install in your pre‑prod. Full rollout depends on scale.
[03:48] Rachel Kim: Pricing model — do you charge per‑token in private deployments or is it a licensing/reserved capacity model?
[03:53] Lena Park: For Private on‑prem we typically do a platform fee plus an enterprise license and optional support SLAs. For Dedicated/reserved we do committed capacity pricing. We can model both; for procurement they like a fixed component for budgeting.
[04:03] Anita Bose: One technical detail — our cluster is air‑gapped behind a proxy that allows only whitelisted IPs if we need to pull images. For the offline path, do you provide an offline registry bundle?
[04:12] Marcus Vela: Yes — we provide signed OCI images and an offline registry tarball you can import into Harbor or your internal registry. We also publish a deterministic manifest so you can verify integrity.
[04:20] Derek Shaw: Any precedent customers in defense or national labs you can mention?
[04:24] Lena Park: We can provide references under NDA; we've done regulated on‑prem installs with a couple of national labs and a defense contractor — we'll include anonymized case studies in the security pack.
[04:33] Rachel Kim: Good. A few follow‑ups from procurement: software updates need to be possible without opening long windows for administrators. How do you do rollback/patching offline?
[04:41] Marcus Vela: Each release is a signed artifact with a version. You import it to your registry, run the upgrade job which is orchestrated by the local control plane; it supports canary rollouts across node pools. Rollbacks are supported by deploying prior images. All manifests are immutable.
[04:52] Anita Bose: Does Redwood provide a policy engine for routing requests by model versions and fallback rules? We want to be sure in case high‑cost models are not available we fallback to a smaller on‑prem model.
[04:59] Lena Park: Yes we support routing policies: you can pin a route to a model family and define automatic fallback to quantized variants or CPU fallback. Policies are configured in the control plane UI or via YAML.
[05:10] Rachel Kim: On model licensing — any restrictions on running open models or fine‑tuned variants?
[05:14] Marcus Vela: You can run open models and your proprietary fine‑tuned models. For Redwoods' curated models, licensing may vary; we'll include license docs. For anything ITAR‑sensitive you can keep models entirely internal.
[05:24] Derek Shaw: A question about chain of custody for artifacts — we need audit trails for who imported a bundle and when.
[05:30] Marcus Vela: Audit logs capture import events, user principals (SSO), and checksums; they can be shipped to your SIEM.
[05:36] Anita Bose: Are there any parts of Redwood that require external DNS/TLS validation? Our network team is picky about external CAs.
[05:42] Lena Park: For air‑gapped installs you can use your internal CA. The platform accepts custom CA bundles. External DNS is not required — you can map internal hostnames.
[05:50] Rachel Kim: Fine. Last thing — can you support an offline model update cadence, like quarterly model refreshes, and will that require re‑validation each time?
[05:58] Marcus Vela: Quarterly refreshes are common. We recommend a staging validation each time — an automated test suite with your acceptance criteria. If the model family changes (e.g., 8‑bit to 4‑bit quantized), we recommend a smoke test for quality regression.
[06:10] Lena Park: Okay, sounds like we have alignment on the big pieces. We'll send over the security pack and the offline install runbook.
[06:16] Rachel Kim: Thanks. One ask — can we get an itemized runbook that our SOC can approve?
[06:20] Lena Park: Yes we'll include a SOC‑friendly checklist.
[06:22] Derek Shaw: Great.
[06:24] Lena Park: Any final questions?
[06:26] Anita Bose: None from me.
[06:28] Rachel Kim: Not right now.
[06:30] Lena Park: Thanks everyone. Recap: Lena to share SOC2 and security pack, Marcus to size hardware options, schedule deep dive for week of 12/14.
[06:40] Meeting end.
